identity.title: The State of the Molecular Gas in Post-starburst Galaxies

paper_type_evidence.quote: We present CO (3–2) observations for three post-starburst galaxies, and dense gas HCN/HCO$^+$/HNC (1–0) observations for six (four new) post-starburst galaxies.

In this work, we aim to explore the molecular gas state of post-starburst galaxies by studying their CO excitation and by using multiple tracers of the dense molecular gas from observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).

question.value: What physical properties and excitation states of the molecular gas in post-starburst galaxies prevent their large gas reservoirs from collapsing and forming stars?

evidence.quote: The observation of large CO-traced molecular gas reservoirs remaining in post-starburst galaxies raises the question of why they have become quiescent and what prevents the CO-traced molecular gas from forming stars.

This absence of detected dense gas raises the new question of what physical properties in the diffuse molecular gas are preventing its collapse into forming stars: Is the gas heated? Is it kinematically disturbed?

results_numeric.quantity: sSFR vs post-burst age two-slope fit (early slope, late slope, pivot point)

evidence.quote: For the sSFR - age comparison, the best fit early slope is 65 Myr, the best fit late slope is 480 Myr, and the pivot point is 77 Myr.

findings_qualitative.value: Post-starburst galaxies have low CO excitation up to CO (3-2), similar to early-type galaxies and lower than starbursts/LIRGs, indicating low gas densities and low kinetic temperatures.

evidence.quote: The post-starbursts have low excitation traced by the CO spectral line energy distribution (SLED) up to CO (3–2), more similar to early-type than starburst galaxies.

findings_qualitative.value: Post-starburst galaxies have high mean ISRF intensity <U> (high dust temperatures) despite low CO excitation, indicating decoupled dust and molecular gas temperatures.

evidence.quote: The post-starburst galaxies lie in an unusual region of this parameter space, having high $\langle U \rangle$ values similar to LIRGs, but low CO excitation, indicating the dust and gas temperatures are not well-coupled.

findings_qualitative.value: CO (3-2) emission is compact (half-light radii 267-400 pc), on average 6.3x smaller than the SDSS r-band optical sizes, placing the galaxies 2.5 sigma below the Kennicutt-Schmidt relation.

evidence.quote: On average, the CO (3–2) sizes are 6.3$\times$ smaller than the $r$-band sizes from the SDSS imaging.

If we define the scatter in the star formation rate surface densities relative to the best-fit relation from (cite: Kennicutt2021) as $\sigma$, the median post-starburst galaxy is 2.5$\sigma$ below the median for the comparison samples

findings_qualitative.value: S02 exhibits a blueshifted CO (3-2) outflow aligned with a blueshifted ionized gas component in MaNGA and an HST dust lane, indicating a multiphase outflow.

evidence.quote: One galaxy displays a blueshifted outflow traced by CO (3–2). MaNGA observations show that the ionized gas velocity is disturbed relative to the stellar velocity field, with a blueshifted component aligned with the molecular gas outflow, suggestive of a multiphase outflow.

findings_qualitative.value: Five out of six post-starburst galaxies have low L'_HCO+/L'_CO ratios (<0.04), except for the youngest galaxy R02, showing that low SFRs are explained by a lack of dense molecular gas.

evidence.quote: Most (5/6) of the post-starburst galaxies have low (${L^{\prime}}_{\rm\!\!HCO+}$/${L^{\prime}}_{\rm\!\!CO}$$<0.04$) fractions, except for R02, which is the youngest post-starburst galaxy in our ALMA-targeted sample.
This is consistent with our previous work (cite: French2018b) and indicates that the low SFRs in the post-starburst phase are due to a lack of dense gas

claims.hypothesis: Low star formation efficiencies in post-starburst galaxies are caused by low molecular gas densities rather than high kinetic temperatures.
claims.experiment: Combine ALMA CO (3-2) observations with IRAM 30m CO (1-0) and CO (2-1) data for three post-starburst galaxies to construct CO SLEDs and model excitation with RADEX.
claims.result: Post-starburst galaxies show low CO excitation consistent with early-type galaxies, with RADEX models favoring log(n) ~ 3.4-3.8 cm^-3 and T ~ 15-30 K.
claims.finding: Lower gas density rather than high kinetic temperature suppresses star formation during the post-starburst phase.

evidence.quote: The low excitation indicates that lower density rather than high temperatures may suppress star formation during the post-starburst phase, as higher temperatures would result in excitation states more like starbursts. Radiative transfer modelling with RADEX supports this picture; the RADEX models favor low densities ($\log n/\rm{cm}^{-3} \sim 3.4-3.8$) and temperatures ($T\sim 15-30$ K),

claims.hypothesis: Post-starburst galaxies lie offset below the Kennicutt-Schmidt relation regardless of whether optical or infrared SFR tracers are used.
claims.experiment: Measure CO (3-2) half-light radii with ALMA and compute Sigma_H2 and Sigma_SFR using Halpha, TIR, and [NeII]+[NeIII] SFR tracers to compare with star-forming and starburst galaxies.
claims.result: CO (3-2) sizes are 267-400 pc (6.3x smaller than r-band sizes), and median post-starburst galaxies lie 2.5 sigma (Halpha), 2.1 sigma (TIR), and 1.9 sigma (Neon) below comparison samples.
claims.finding: Post-starburst galaxies have high molecular gas surface densities for their SFR surface densities, and this offset is not driven by dust-obscured star formation.

evidence.quote: When using the TIR luminosity to trace SFR, we find the median post-starburst galaxy to be 2.1$\sigma$ below the median for the comparison samples and 3.3$\sigma$ below the median for the starburst sample alone; when using the Neon-based SFRs, we find the median post-starburst galaxy to be 1.9$\sigma$ below the median for the comparison samples

We find this same result using both optical (H$\alpha$) and infrared SFR tracers (TIR luminosity and \[NeII\] 12.8$\mu$m + \[NeIII\] 15.6$\mu$m), indicating that this offset is not driven by the presence of dust-obscured star formation.

claims.hypothesis: The southeastern blueshifted CO (3-2) component in S02 is a multiphase molecular and ionized gas outflow rather than disk rotation or merger infall.
claims.experiment: Fit 3D tilted ring models with Barolo to CO (3-2) kinematics in S02 and compare with MaNGA stellar and ionized velocity maps and HST imaging.
claims.result: The component at -64 to -108 km/s shows excess flux above the Barolo rotation model, lacks a symmetric northwest counterpart, exceeds stellar velocity, and aligns with a 40 km/s blueshifted ionized gas component and dust lane, yielding M_outflow = 7.3e7 M_sun and dM/dt = 16 M_sun/yr.
claims.finding: S02 hosts a multiphase outflow with kinetic power (8e40 erg/s) consistent with low-luminosity AGN/LINERs or TDEs and mass loss rate matching statistical CO depletion.

evidence.quote: Thus, while the blueshifted component is aligned with the stellar velocity field and bulk rotation of the molecular gas, it is more likely to be an outflow than an extension of the molecular gas rotation

The MaNGA observations show the ionized gas velocity is disturbed relative to the stellar velocity field, with a blueshifted component aligned with the molecular gas outflow, indicative of a possible multiphase outflow.

claims.hypothesis: Low star formation rates in post-starburst galaxies are explained by a low fraction of dense molecular gas relative to total molecular gas throughout the post-starburst phase.
claims.experiment: Observe HCN, HCO+, and HNC (1-0) in four post-starburst galaxies with ALMA Band 3, combine with two literature galaxies, and compare L'_HCO+/L'_CO and L'_HCO+ vs SFR against comparison samples.
claims.result: 5 of 6 post-starburst galaxies have L'_HCO+/L'_CO < 0.04 (statistically distinct from comparison samples at 2 sigma via Mann-Whitney U test), except the youngest galaxy R02, and L'_HCO+ matches their low SFRs (except H03).
claims.finding: Low SFRs in the post-starburst phase are due to a lack of dense gas, with possible rapid early evolution in dense gas fraction, though a larger sample is needed to confirm the evolutionary timescale.

evidence.loc: Star Formation in the Dense Gas
evidence.quote: We can exclude the possibility that the post-starbursts and comparison samples are drawn from the same distribution in HCO$+$/CO at the $2\sigma$ level

Low ratios of HCO$^+$/CO, indicating low fractions of dense molecular gas relative to the total molecular gas, are seen throughout the post-starburst phase beginning $\sim$10-200 Myr after burst ends for 5/6 post-starbust galaxies.

why_this_data.value: Previous dense gas studies only yielded upper limits in two galaxies; detections of dense gas tracers across the full post-starburst age baseline (including younger PCA-selected galaxies) and CO (3-2) observations were required to measure gas excitation and dense gas fractions.

evidence.quote: In order to address these questions, we require detections (rather than limits) of the dense gas tracers in post-starburst galaxies.
The inclusion of two galaxies from the (cite: Rowlands2015) sample allows for a wider post-starburst age baseline for this sample.

why_this_method.value: HCO+ (1-0) is used as the primary dense gas mass tracer rather than HCN (1-0) because HCN can be enhanced by mechanical heating, cosmic rays, IR pumping, or XDR chemistry; Halpha SFRs are used as primary because they are unbiased compared to Neon SFRs and available for the full sample.

evidence.quote: We use H$\alpha$-based star formation rates (SFRs) for the post-starburst galaxies from (cite: French2015) and (cite: Rowlands2015) as this measurement is the least biased and most available SFR for our post-starburst sample.

In several cases, the post-starburst galaxies show evidence that the ${L^{\prime}}_{\rm\!\!HCN}$ luminosity is enhanced relative to the ${L^{\prime}}_{\rm\!\!HCO+}$, similar to many AGN and ULIRGs (see further discussion in §3.6), so we consider ${L^{\prime}}_{\rm\!\!HCO+}$ here as a more accurate tracer of the dense gas mass.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: High kinetic temperature with low density as the cause of low SFE (rejected because it would produce high CO excitation, contrary to observations).

evidence.quote: The first possibility is high kinetic temperatures in the gas paired with low gas densities; in this case, we would expect to see high gas excitation throughout the post-starburst phase.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Expanding sphere or plane parallel slab geometries in RADEX (not used as they do not provide substantially different results from a uniform sphere).

evidence.quote: Assuming alternate geometries of an expanding sphere or plane parallel slab will not provide substantially different results for this application (cite: Krips2011).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Rotation or merger-driven gas infall as the origin of the blueshifted CO (3-2) component in S02 (rejected due to lack of symmetric counterpart, excess over Barolo model and stellar velocity, and coalesced smooth stellar velocity field).

evidence.quote: Thus, while the blueshifted component is aligned with the stellar velocity field and bulk rotation of the molecular gas, it is more likely to be an outflow than an extension of the molecular gas rotation
The blueshifted component is unlikely to be a parcel of infalling gas from the recent merger, as the smooth stellar velocity field suggests any merger components have already coalesced.

limitations_admitted.value: Inferred density and temperature from RADEX are highly degenerate when only J <= 3 CO lines are sampled and cannot rule out a secondary warm/hot molecular gas component.

evidence.quote: The inferred density and temperature values are highly degenerate unless the full rise and turnover of the CO SLED can be sampled (cite: Carilli2013; Kamenetzky2018).

The cold molecular gas temperatures indicated by the low CO excitation do not preclude the existence of an additional component of warm or hot gas, as the low J CO lines cannot predict the full SLED in the event of a secondary component of high temperature molecular gas.

limitations_admitted.value: Combining single-dish IRAM 30m and interferometric ALMA measurements introduces ~37% flux uncertainty.

evidence.quote: For H02 and H03, the ALMA and IRAM CO (2–1) measurements differ by $\sim37$% (consistent within 1.5$\sigma$ of the combined uncertainty).

limitations_admitted.value: More than 50% of the CO (3-2) flux in H02 and H03 is contained within a central unresolved beam.

evidence.quote: as $>50$% of the flux is contained within a central unresolved beamsize in both tracers for both galaxies.

limitations_admitted.value: The rapid early decline in L'_HCO+/L'_CO with post-burst age is driven by a single young galaxy (R02), requiring a larger sample to confirm.

evidence.quote: This may indicate a rapid ($<<100$ Myr) decline in the dense gas fraction at the start of the starburst, but a larger sample will be required to determine whether this trend is significant, as it is driven by the observations for a single galaxy.

limitations_admitted.value: Cannot fully rule out an obscured nuclear starburst (SFR ~ 5 M_sun yr^-1) in H02 and H03 where TIR SFRs strongly exceed Halpha SFRs and mid-IR Neon spectroscopy is unavailable.

evidence.quote: but we cannot fully rule out the possibility of an obscured region with SFR$\sim5$ M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ in H02 and H03.

referee_caveats_inferred: Combining single-dish IRAM 30m CO(1-0)/(2-1) fluxes with 1.5 arcsec aperture ALMA CO(3-2) fluxes without matching beams or uv-tapering can bias the CO SLED ratios.
RADEX modeling of HCN and HCO+ relies on a fixed [X/CO] = 10^-4 abundance ratio and assumes identical spatial filling factors for CO and dense gas tracers.
Outflow mass and energetics in S02 assume the standard Galactic CO-to-H2 conversion factor applies equally to the outflowing gas as to the central disk.
